sweep_summary: Seven title hits, two already the catalog's deciding sources (K&AK 1980, McCarthy 1980; re-read in the held SLS 10 scanned, and an open IDEALS copy of the volume was downloaded, though its text layer drops the K&AK p.55 paragraph). New open full text: Nasr 1959 (Phonetica 4: 89-94) via the archive.org Phonetica scan, a first-hand Beirut description whose Patterns 1-4 state exactly the catalog rule (rightmost heavy with final CVC light, else initial, antepenult limit in four-light-syllable words) and add secondary stress on other long syllables — confirms/refines, does not supersede K&AK. Chahal 2001 (Melbourne thesis) is intonation; PDF restricted to UniMelb logins, abstract silent on placement. Brame 1974 (LI 5) and Brame 1973 (Halle festschrift) are print/lending-only and concern Palestinian Arabic, whose rule K&AK already restate on p.55; Abu-Salim 1982 dissertation has no open copy (IDEALS lacks it) and is probably Palestinian too. catalog's classification stands as 'weight'; no contradiction found.

new_statements.quote: Long syllable. A long syllable is one that contains a vowel cluster ... or one vowel followed by a consonant cluster ... cvv, cvvc, cvvcc, or cvcc. Short syllable. A short syllable is one that contains one vowel followed either by nothing or by one consonant. cv or cvc. ... Beginning with the end of a word and moving back, the first long syllable takes primary stress; the other long syllables (if any) take secondary stress; all short syllables (if any) take tertiary stress. ... The first syllable in a word containing two or three short syllables takes primary stress; the rest take tertiary stress. ... The third syllable in a word containing four short syllables takes primary stress; the rest take tertiary stress.

new_statements.reading: A 1959 first-hand description (author based in Beirut) of a Lebanese dialect: primary stress on the rightmost syllable whose vowel is followed by VV or two consonants in the string (equivalently the rightmost heavy syllable, with word-final CVC counting as light and final CVCC/CVVC as heavy); if there is none, initial stress in words of two or three light syllables and antepenultimate stress in words of four (examples [kamašítu], [sa?alítak]), i.e. never further left than the antepenult. Also reports secondary stress on the other long syllables ([Tàawúus], [sìžžàadáatna]) and a footnote that a second dialect keeps stress in place after -ha becomes -a (kamáša). Confirms the catalog's weight coding in every clause and refines its secondary-stress note ('none reported') with a report of secondary stress on non-primary long syllables.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction. Minor refinements only: (1) Nasr's 'long syllable' is defined string-wise (vowel followed by a consonant cluster), so a non-final CVC counts long and a word-final CVC short -- the reader's equivalence to the catalog's 'CVC light only in final position' is exact and is borne out by the marked forms [kàssártu], [ʔawàamírna] (non-final CVC stressed) vs [sáaʔil], [sáʔalit], [sámak] (final CVC unstressed). (2) Nasr states the antepenult limit only for words of exactly four short syllables (Pattern 4: [kamašítu], [saʔalítak]); he gives no general 'never beyond the antepenult' stateme…

audit.reasoning: (1) Every fragment of the deciding quotation was found verbatim at the stated pages in the held SLS 10 scanned (K&AK p.55, p.57, p.64; McCarthy pp.78-79), with the page images we hold covering pp.57/64/79; the only wrinkle is the record's '[scanned] Assiuming' vs the file's 'Assiuning'. (2) The classification rests on two 1980 theoretical phonology articles (McCarthy on Damascene; Kenstowicz & native-speaker Abdul-Karim on Levantine/Beirut), and is independently corroborated by the standard reference grammar we hold (Cowell 1964 p.18: last 'long' syllable accented, else the first; long = long vowel or V+CC, so final CVC is not long and final CVCC/CVVC is) and by Kager 2009's EALL survey (held), and now by Kelly 2021 (downloaded, section 1.1.1) which restates the identical rule citing McCarthy 1979, Abdul-Karim 1980, Chahal 2001, Watson 2011. StressTyp2's partial mismatch noted in the record is a database para

sources.quote: Long syllable. A long syllable is one that contains a vowel cluster (the same vowel geminated or two different vowels) or one vowel followed by a consonant cluster (the same consonant geminated or two different consonants). cvv, cvvc, cvvcc, or cvcc. Short syllable. A short syllable is one that contains one vowel followed either by nothing or by one consonant. cv or cvc. [p. 89] ... Beginning with the end of a word and moving back, the first long syllable takes primary stress; the other long syllables (if any) take secondary stress; all short syllables (if any) take tertiary stress. ... The first syllable in a word containing two or three short syllables takes primary stress ... [p. 91] The third syllable in a word containing four short syllables takes primary stress [p. 92]
sources.note: First-hand description of one Beirut-area dialect (author at Beirut College for Women). Primary stress on the rightmost 'long' syllable, where long = V followed by VV/VC-C in the string (so a CVC syllable followed by another consonant counts as long, but word-final CVC is short and final CVCC/CVVC is long); if no long syllable, the first syllable in 2-3-syllable words and the third (= antepenult) in 4-syllable words. Examples with marks on the page images: [mása], [sámak], [kámašu], [sá?alit], [kamašítu], [sa?alítak], [kamášha], [hašáRha], [?awàamírna], [sìžžàadáatna]. Also reports secondary…

sources.citation: Kelly, Niamh E. 2021. Syllable weight, vowel length and focus in Lebanese Arabic. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 6(1): 142. doi:10.16995/glossa.5727 (CC-BY; live site behind an Anubis bot wall, Internet Archive copy of the HTML full text and the JATS XML galley. the the Internet Archive PDF galley is truncated at 1 MiB and unreadable)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In Arabic, stress assignment is determined by syllable weight. Lexical stress in Lebanese Arabic is described as falling on: a word-final superheavy syllable, then on a heavy penult, then for disyllabic words ending in CV or CVC, on the initial syllable, and otherwise on the antepenult, whether heavy or light (McCarthy 1979; Abdul-Karim 1980; Chahal 2001; Watson 2011). In final position, CVVC has been analyzed as the final C being extrametrical (Watson 2011).'
sources.note: Open-access instrumental study whose background section restates the Lebanese stress rule exactly as coded (superheavy final > heavy penult > initial in disyllables > antepenult 'whether heavy or light'); downloaded now, confirms.

sources.citation: McCarthy, John J. 1980. A note on the accentuation of Damascene Arabic. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 10(2): 77-98.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable when it is heavy (7a) and in disyllables (7b). Otherwise stress falls on the antepenult (7c). Forms like muttafaide 'united (f. sg.)' borrowed from Literary Arabic show that stress does not retract to the preantepenult even when the penult and the antepenult are light. Finally, the examples in (7d) display the characteristic stressing of a superheavy ultima.
sources.note: Damascene: superheavy ultima > heavy penult (and disyllables) > antepenult; no preantepenultimate stress. Matches the catalog's weight coding.

sources.citation: Chahal, Dana. 2003. Phonetic cues to prominence in Lebanese Arabic. Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (Barcelona), 2067-2070.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Instrumental study of the acoustic correlates (F0, duration, RMS, F1/F2) of lexical stress vs pitch accent vs nuclear accent in Lebanese Arabic; test words are disyllabic CV.CV with 'lexical stress falling on the penultimate syllable in each word'; concludes Arabic is 'a stress-accent language, similar to English'. Does not restate the placement algorithm.
sources.note: Acoustic evidence that Lebanese lexical stress is phonetically real (duration, F0, RMS, formants) independent of pitch accent; supports treating the described pattern as word stress; downloaded now, silent on placement.

sources.quote: The proposed model of Lebanese Arabic intonation (chapter 2) posits a prosodic hierarchy for the language, which comprises three prominence levels- lexical stress, pitch accent and nuclear accent, and three intonationally-relevant prosodic constituents- the intonational phrase, the intermediate phrase and the prosodic word. ... Pitch accents can be monotonal or bitonal, and associate to lexically stressed syllables
sources.note: Abstract: an AM intonation model plus acoustic study of prominence levels and boundaries; treats lexical stress as the anchor of pitch accents but the abstract states no placement rule. Kelly 2021 (downloaded earlier, held by the project here) cites Chahal 2001 among the sources for the standard Lebanese rule (final superheavy > heavy penult > initial in disyllables > antepenult), so chapter 2 presumably restates it. Instrumental companion Chahal 2003 (ICPhS) is already held by the project.
